paper_title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same underlying identity. Records may refer to the same identity despite differences in presentation, whereas superficially similar records may refer to different identities. This problem is studied both in human identity verification from *Corresponding author. 1 faces and voices (Smith et al., 2025) and in finegrained object discrimination by vision-language models (Marsili et al., 2026). The latter shows that models can incorrectly match objects that share salient visual features but differ in local structure. We focus on multimodal identity matching, where each record describes an object through an image and text, and the model determines whether two records match. Yet what counts as "the same" depends on the target granularity. Cognitive research shows that categorization rules modulate shape representations in the human visual cortex (Henderson et al., 2025). In computer vision, conditional image similarity likewise requires models to compare images according to specified attributes or objects (Vaze et al., 2023). E-commerce provides concrete and challenging setting for studying multi-granularity identity matching. Differences in photography, title wording, and attribute expressions across sellers introduce substantial variation in presentation. We adopt two nested matching criteria. At the base level, records must describe the same underlying design and agree on its core attributes, while differences are permitted in specified set of additional attributes. At the variant level, records must additionally agree on all attributes in this set. This matching granularity corresponds to the instance-level exact matching setting in Pailitao-VL (Chen et al., 2026). As illustrated in Figure 1(a), records and do not match at the base level because of the structural difference between flat and kitten-heel shoes (Case 1). Within shared base design, records that differ in color (Case 2) or heel height (Case 3) do not match at the variant level. variant-level match therefore implies base-level match, but not conversely. These examples illustrate central challenge in identity matching: models must acquire and interpret multimodal evidence, compare attributes across records, and determine which differences should affect the matching decision Figure 1: Multi-granularity identity matching and the PURE task taxonomy. (a) Records and differ in heel structure and do not match at the base level (Case 1). Within shared base design, records that differ in color (Case 2) or heel height (Case 3) do not match at the variant level. (b) PURE organizes 14 tasks by diagnostic dimension and identity-matching granularity. at the target granularity. Recent MLLM benchmarks assess visual perception, multi-image comparison, and comparative reasoning (Fu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). In e-commerce, benchmarks cover multimodal understanding, product matching, and rule-aware relevance assessment (Ling et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025). However, in direct identity matching, final accuracy does not separately characterize model performance on the capabilities involved. We therefore introduce PURE1, diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching, comprising 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks in four dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Judgment. The questions are derived from real-world e-commerce pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten MLLMs, Understanding is strongest on average, whereas Judgment is weakest. Modality ablations reveal task-specific evidence dependence and suggest that models can mistake non-discriminative textual differences for identity conflicts. In direct matching, most models achieve higher recall on matching pairs than on non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. Overall 1The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/ datasets/alibaba-multimodal-industrial-ai/PURE, and alibaba-multimodal-industrial-ai/PURE. https://github.com/ evaluation code the at PURE Scores also correlate with performance on direct identity matching and two independently constructed benchmarks. Together, these findings show that PURE complements aggregate matching accuracy by revealing capability gaps, dependence on input evidence, and distinct patterns across matching granularities. Our contributions are as follows: multi-granularity diagnostic benchmark. We formalize multimodal identity matching under base-level and variant-level criteria, defining 14 tasks across four capability dimensions (3.1). An error-driven construction pipeline. We construct questions from misclassified real-world record pairs, combining task assignment, multimodel screening, and verification by two domain experts (3.2). Empirical findings on identity matching. Experiments with ten MLLMs reveal gap between attribute understanding and identity judgment, task-specific evidence dependence, and matching asymmetries across granularities (4).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Fine-grained visual comparison and identity matching. Fine-grained visual comparison examines whether models can identify subtle differences and correspondences across images. Product1M, M5Product, and FGPR study multimodal product representations and retrieval (Zhan et al., 2 Table 1: Comparison with closely related benchmarks. Evidence modalities indicate the modalities required for models to answer questions. Identity matching indicates whether at least one task explicitly evaluates identity matching. Multi-granularity matching indicates whether identity matching is evaluated at multiple levels of granularity. Benchmark Evidence modalities Identity matching Multi-granularity matching Evaluation focus M4Bench (Ye et al., 2025) FGVQA (Marsili et al., 2026) VLM-SubtleBench (Kim et al., 2026) EcomMMMU (Ling et al., 2025) RAIR (Lu et al., 2025) OxyEcomBench (Liu et al., 2026) PURE Images Images Images Images, text Images, text Images, text Images, text Visual comparison Fine-grained recognition Subtle comparative reasoning E-commerce understanding Search relevance Broad e-commerce tasks Capabilities for identity matching 2021; Dong et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026). Pailitao-VL evaluates exact matching at granularity corresponding to our variant level (Chen et al., 2026). BLINK and MIBench assess visual perception and multi-image understanding (Fu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), while MLLM-CompBench, M4Bench, and VLM-SubtleBench evaluate crossimage comparison and fine-grained discrimination (Kil et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). FGVQA evaluates fine-grained recognition across six datasets (Marsili et al., 2026). NaturalBench pairs each question with two images that require different answers, assessing whether models use visual evidence rather than rely on language priors (Li et al., 2024). However, these visual comparison benchmarks do not evaluate identity matching under separate base-level and variant-level criteria. E-commerce benchmarks. Existing benchmarks in e-commerce cover diverse tasks, including product understanding, matching, and search relevance. Shopping MMLU evaluates textual shopping skills (Jin et al., 2024), while EcomMMMU and OxyEcomBench cover diverse multimodal e-commerce tasks (Ling et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). For industrial applications, IndustryBench evaluates LLMs on multilingual industrial procurement question answering (Bai et al., 2026). IndustryBench-MIPU evaluates MLLMs on attribute value extraction from multiple industrial product images (Qi et al., 2026). RAIR evaluates rule-aware search relevance (Lu et al., 2025). TaoSR1 includes an atomic capability benchmark covering four dimensions of relevance modeling (Dong et al., 2026). However, identity matching is not central focus of these benchmarks. When included, it is evaluated as one of several application tasks, without dedicated assessment of the capabilities supporting identity matching. Table 1 compares the scope and focus of closely related benchmarks. PURE assesses evidence acquisition, attribute understanding, cross-record comparison, and evidence-grounded judgment for identity matching at the base and variant levels, providing capability profiles that complement final matching results.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: We define identity matching at the base and variant levels and design 14 evaluation tasks across four capability dimensions (Section 3.1). We then describe how questions are constructed from realworld matching errors, screened, verified, and assembled into the final benchmark (Section 3.2).

sections.title: 3.1 PURE Framework
sections.content: Matching granularity specifies which properties must agree for two records to match. The task taxonomy organizes the assessment into four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Judgment. We instantiate these tasks with e-commerce records containing images, titles, and attribute descriptions.

sections.title: Matching
sections.content: We study identity matching over two multimodal records, each of which may contain images, descriptive text, and structured attributes. We define two nested matching criteria that differ in what counts as the same identity rather than in the input format. 3 Two records match at the base level when they refer to the same underlying design: their identitydefining structure, composition, and core attributes are equivalent, while differences confined to specified set of additional attributes are permitted. Presentation differences such as viewpoint, background, seller-specific wording, and marketing layout do not change their base-level identity. Two records match at the variant level when they match at the base level and additionally agree on all applicable attributes in this set. Writing for match between records and at granularity g, we have variant = base b, (1) whereas the converse need not hold: two records may match at the base level but differ at the variant level. For example, two listings of the same shoe design in different colors can match at the base level but differ at the variant level. Listings from different sellers can still match at the variant level when they describe the same design and agree on all specified attributes despite differences in imagery or wording. Identity-matching systems typically produce either pairwise same/different prediction or similarity score used for retrieval. These outputs characterize the final matching outcome but do not show how well model performs the individual tasks involved. matching error may involve missed visual detail, misunderstood attribute expression, an incorrect cross-record comparison, or the misapplication of an identity rule. PURE therefore complements direct matching evaluation with taskspecific questions that assess these capabilities separately. Each PURE question follows multiple-choice format and consists of task-specific evidence, question stem, answer options, and reference answer. Depending on the task, the model-visible evidence is drawn from listing images, titles, and descriptions of the selected variants attributes.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Task Taxonomy
sections.content: PURE comprises 14 tasks across two matching granularities, organized into four dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Judgment. These dimensions assess evidence acquisition, semantic interpretation and normalization, comparative reasoning and consistency, and the application of identity criteria, respectively. Perception. Perception examines whether model can acquire identity-relevant evidence before comparing products. Fine-Grained Visual Recognition (A1) identifies local appearance and structural cues, Product Image OCR (A2) reads text printed on products and packaging, and ImageText Evidence Extraction (A3) extracts identity-relevant attributes from product image and its corresponding title. Understanding. Understanding examines whether product evidence can be interpreted and normalized. Attribute Expression Equivalence (B1) identifies semantically equivalent attribute expressions; Primary Product and Bundle Relations (B2) distinguishes the primary product from accessories and bundle components; and Product Title Attribute Interpretation (B3) resolves product terminology, model expressions, and title attributes. At the variant level, Textual Core Attribute Extraction (B4) identifies the selected variants core attributes from the title and attribute text, resolving ambiguity or conflicting descriptions. Variant-Level Attribute Equivalence (B5) determines whether two selected variants have semantically equivalent attribute descriptions despite surface-form differences. Reasoning. Reasoning examines differences and consistency across product evidence. Visual Difference Localization (C1) identifies or rules out identity-relevant visual differences, while CrossProduct Attribute Conflict Detection (C2) detects identity-relevant attribute conflicts between two product listings. Contrastive Attribute Grounding (C3) evaluates two similar products against two competing attribute descriptions as four-question group. Variant-Level Visual Equivalence (C4) determines whether two images depict the same identity at the variant level by distinguishing identityrelevant visual differences from changes in presentation. Judgment. Judgment examines whether model can apply identity criteria to identify the non-match rules supported by record pair. Base-Level Rule Judgment (D1) asks which base-level non-match rule, if any, the pair triggers. Variant-Level Rule Judgment (D2) identifies which variant-level nonmatch rule, if any, record pair triggers. Both tasks include an option indicating that no rule applies, allowing the model to distinguish pairs with supported conflict from those that satisfy the matching Figure 2: Construction pipeline of PURE. ❶ Real-world base-level and variant-level record pairs jointly misclassified by an embedding matcher and generative MLLM form the source pool. ❷ Identity criteria and the task taxonomy guide evidence-grounded analysis and task assignment. ❸ Gemini 3.1 Pro generates task-conditioned questions. ❹ Candidates undergo multi-model quality screening followed by expert review. criterion. The task taxonomy is developed through human analysis of identity rules and recurrent matching errors. The complete taxonomy is reported in Table 4 in Appendix A, including each tasks name, dimension-aligned identifiers, target identitymatching granularity, evidence configurations, and primary diagnostic focus. Figure 1(b) visualizes its organization across dimension and granularity.

sections.title: 3.2 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Having defined the target identity-matching decision and its tasks, we construct PURE through four stages: ❶ Real-World Data Collection, ❷ Evidence-Grounded Task Assignment, ❸ Question Generation, and ❹ Quality Assurance.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Real-World Data Collection
sections.content: We begin with real-world e-commerce record pairs labeled under base-level or variant-level matching criteria. To identify challenging cases, each pair is evaluated by two distinct matching paradigms. An embedding-based matcher encodes the records independently and derives decision from their representation similarity, whereas generative MLLM jointly observes both records and predicts whether they match at the designated granularity. We retain pairs for which both matchers disagree with the reference label at that granularity. The retained pool covers false-positive and false-negative cases at both levels. This intersection emphasizes errors shared by two substantially different matching mechanisms. The resulting pairs provide source material for constructing questions about the evidence and capabilities involved in these difficult decisions.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Evidence-Grounded Task Assignment
sections.content: Each retained pair is assigned to one predefined task before question generation. As illustrated in Figure 2, Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026a) receives the original record evidence, the reference matching label at the designated granularity, the two matcher outputs, the applicable identity criteria, and the task definitions. It produces structured assignment record that identifies the evidence supporting the reference decision and recommends the task most relevant to interpreting that evidence correctly. The assignment record and selected evidence are retained for question generation and subsequent expert verification. For variant-level pairs labeled as matches in the retained pool, which the generative matcher incorrectly predicts as non-matches, we additionally use evidence-alignment probes to inform task assignment. sections.title: 3.2.3 Question Generation
sections.content: For each assigned case, Gemini 3.1 Pro receives the target task specification, applicable identity criteria, selected source evidence, and the assignment record. It generates multiple-choice question with its answer options and reference answer. Questions in product image OCR (A2) and imagetext evidence extraction (A3) allow multiple selections, whereas the other tasks require single selected Inspired by the grouped evaluation deoption. sign of NaturalBench (Li et al., 2024), the contrastive attribute grounding task (C3) combines two related records with two discriminative attribute statements. Each record is queried about both statements, yielding four questions whose responses jointly constitute one scoring unit. This structure assesses consistent attribute grounding across the two records.

sections.title: 3.2.4 Quality Assurance
sections.content: Quality assurance has two stages. First, Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a), Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026b) independently screen each candidate for evidence sufficiency, option completeness, unique answer support, and consistency with its assigned task and identity granularity. candidate proceeds only when at least two models accept it. This stage retains approximately 72% of roughly 3,940 candidate questions, yielding 2,819 questions for expert review. Second, two qualified e-commerce domain experts review every surviving unit against the source evidence and applicable identity criteria. Units that fail any review criterion are removed, and disagreements are resolved by jointly re-examining the source evidence. unit is retained only when both experts approve it. Following expert review and final task-wise assembly, the benchmark contains 1,457 questions corresponding to 1,367 scoring units, including 30 complete C3 groups. Reviewer qualifications, detailed instructions, and count definitions are provided in Appendix D.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate PURE through three research questions. RQ1 characterizes MLLM performance across tasks and capability dimensions. RQ2 tests models dependence on visual and textual evidence. RQ3 examines whether PURE scores align with direct identity matching and independently constructed external benchmarks, while characterizing granularity-dependent behavior in direct matching.

sections.title: 4.1.1 Baselines
sections.content: We evaluate ten recent MLLMs, including closedsource models and open-source models of dif6 ferent sizes. The closed-source baselines are Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026b), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), and Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026b). The open-source baselines are four Qwen3.5 variants (9B, 27B, 35B-A3B, and 397BA17B) (Qwen Team, 2026a), DeepSeek-V4.1Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026).

sections.title: 4.2 Capability Profiles (RQ1)
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 2 consolidates the overall, dimension-level, and task-level results. Overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%, revealing substantial variation across the evaluated MLLMs. Gemini 3.8 Flash ranks first and leads all four dimensions, and Kimi K3 ranks first among the open-source models. Strengths and weaknesses. Understanding is the strongest dimension for every evaluated model, whereas Judgment is the weakest for most. Models perform consistently well on textual core attribute extraction (B4) and attribute equivalence (B5), but remain less reliable at locating visual differences (C1) and identifying applicable rules at the variant level (D2). These results reveal gap between 2The main comparison primarily uses non-thinking configurations. Paired comparisons with and without thinking are reported in Appendix C.1. understanding attributes and identifying the visual evidence and rules that determine identity. Scaling behavior. The Qwen3.5 series includes dense and mixture-of-experts variants at different parameter scales, with overall scores ranging from 47.1% to 59.2%. The dense 27B model nearly matches 397B-A17B and outperforms 35B-A3B, while 9B still exceeds 35B-A3B on several individual tasks. Moreover, the gains of 27B and 397B-A17B over 9B and 35B-A3B are larger in Perception and Understanding than in Reasoning and Judgment. Additional capacity is therefore associated more consistently with acquiring and interpreting evidence, while applying identity criteria remains shared weakness. Takeaway: Models are more accurate at extracting and interpreting attributes than at localizing visual differences or applying identity criteria.

sections.title: 4.3 Evidence Dependence under Modality
sections.content: Ablation (RQ2) We conduct paired modality ablations on A3, C2, and D1, covering evidence extraction, cross-record comparison, and rule judgment. Each question is evaluated under three conditions: full input, without listing images, and without listing titles. Task instructions and answer options remain fixed across conditions. We define = AccFull AccAblated, where {image, title} and positive value indicates decrease in accuracy after evidence removal. These ablations assess how models predictive behavior depends on the supplied evidence. Figure 3 summarizes the ablation results across all ten models. As expected, removing either the image or the title reduces mean accuracy on A3. In C2, removing images reduces mean accuracy by 8.8 percentage points, whereas removing titles increases it by 2.7 points, with six of the ten models showing higher accuracy. In D1, removing images reduces mean accuracy by 17.5 points, whereas removing titles increases it by 8.2 points, and this pattern holds for all ten models. Further analysis shows that removing listing titles increases accuracy when the correct answer is "no applicable rule" but decreases it when the correct answer specifies non-match rule (Appendix C.2). These effects suggest that textual evidence helps models identify valid non-match rules but can also induce false conflict judgments on matching pairs. sections.title: 4.4.2 Relation to External Benchmarks
sections.content: Motivated by VLM-SubtleBenchs model-level relevance analysis (Kim et al., 2026), we compare PURE with two closely related external benchmarks. M4Bench (Ye et al., 2025) includes multiimage product comparison tasks relevant to ecommerce matching, whereas FGVQA (Marsili et al., 2026) evaluates fine-grained visual understanding across six datasets, including instancelevel recognition of retail products. We also report rank correlations between overall scores on PURE and those on each external benchmark across the same ten models. Model-wise scores are provided in Appendix Table 9. The resulting correlations are strong for both M4Bench (ρ = 0.855) and FGVQA (ρ = 0.842). These correlations suggest that PURE captures capability differences that are also reflected in independently constructed benchmarks of e-commerce image comparison and crossdomain fine-grained recognition.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced PURE, diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching, instantiated with real e-commerce records. Its 14 Figure 3: Modality-ablation results across ten MLLMs. Bars show unweighted mean accuracy under the full-input and two ablated conditions, and gray dots denote individual models. Parenthetical values report = AccFull AccAblated in percentage points. echoes the "blind faith in text" observed under controlled cross-modal conflicts (Deng et al., 2025). Takeaway: Current MLLMs benefit from multimodal evidence, yet sometimes mistake nondiscriminative textual differences for identity conflicts.

sections.title: 4.4.1 Relation to Direct Base-Level and
sections.content: Variant-Level Matching To examine the relationship between performance on PURE and direct identity matching, we reuse record pairs from PURE tasks involving two products. The same ten MLLMs directly predict binary labels, judging whether the two products match at the corresponding base or variant level. The evaluation set contains 330 base-level pairs and 211 variant-level pairs, with balanced class distributions, respectively. We report balanced accuracy and class-specific recall in Appendix C.3. Across the ten models, overall scores on PURE show strong Spearman rank correlation (Spearman, 1904) with direct-matching balanced accuracy (ρ = 0.952). Table 3 shows different patterns at the two identity levels. At the base level, eight of ten models achieve higher recall on matching pairs than on non-matching pairs. At the variant level, eight 8 tasks assess Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Judgment at the base and variant levels. Across ten MLLMs, attribute understanding is relative strength, whereas visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment remain weaknesses. Modality ablations reveal task-specific evidence dependence. In direct matching, most models exhibit different recall patterns at the base and variant levels. PURE provides shared benchmark for comparing model capabilities beyond aggregate matching accuracy, guiding progress toward more reliable multimodal identity matching.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: PURE evaluates explicit responses from generative MLLMs and therefore does not directly characterize embedding-based retrieval or end-to-end matching systems. The source pool is drawn from difficult cases shared by particular embeddingbased and generative matchers, which may inherit their coverage biases. Finally, because the benchmark is instantiated with records from specific ecommerce setting, generalization across platforms, languages, product categories, and non-commerce identity domains remains to be established.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: PURE is constructed from real-world e-commerce record pairs containing listing images, titles, and attributes of the selected variant, and is intended for research on multimodal identity matching. Candidate questions were screened using multiple models and verified against the source evidence and task criteria by two experienced e-commerce practitioners. The benchmark may reflect biases in its source systems, category coverage, and listing presentation, and should not be treated as representative of all products or markets.

sections.title: D Human Review Protocol
sections.content: Reviewer background and eligibility. The review was conducted by two domain experts, one woman and one man. Both were practitioners at an e-commerce company with multiple years of experience in product understanding and identitymatching work. Their routine work required interpreting listing images, titles, and attributes of the selected variant under operational matching criteria, and they were therefore qualified to verify the evidence and base-level and variant-level decisions represented in PURE. sections.title: E Prompts
sections.content: The original prompts are in Chinese. English translations are provided below. E.1 Evaluation Prompt and option denotes non-match. The terms "Item" and "SKU" in the original prompts correspond to the base and variant levels defined in this paper, respectively. Direct Matching Prompt You are an evaluator of e-commerce product matching. Determine whether two products belong to the same Item or the same SKU. An Item match requires agreement in core category, brand, product model, structure, and style. Non-essential differences in seller, image background, packaging presentation, and title wording can be ignored. SKU match additionally requires semantic agreement in key sales specifications, including color, size, quantity, and capacity. conflict in any key specification indicates non-match. Use only the images, titles, and SKU attributes provided in this request. Do not use external information. We present the shared system instruction used for benchmark evaluation. Options: A. Match B. Non-match You must strictly follow the JSON format below. Do not include explanations or Markdown code blocks. {"answer": "A or B"} System Prompt You are an expert in visual understanding of e-commerce products. Based on the provided information and question, select the most accurate answer from the given options. For single-choice questions, select only one option letter (e.g., A). For multiple-answer questions, select all correct option letters (e.g., ABC). You must strictly follow the JSON format below. Do not include explanations or Markdown code blocks. {"answer": "Final option letter(s), e.g., or ABC"} E.2 Direct Matching Prompt Direct identity matching uses separate system instruction.
